questions.question: When and where did William H. Ferber (born December 1869, Ohio; husband of Emma Becker Ferber; father of Charles Hubert Ferber, b. 1891, Cincinnati) die?
questions.rationale: This is the project objective directly — a single death event with date and place as its two attributes. William appears alive in the 1900 U.S. census and his name appears alongside Emma in Cincinnati city directories through at least 1903–1910, but no death fact is recorded in the tree. Ohio death records begin in 1908 (statewide), but Hamilton County/Cincinnati records and city directories can bracket his death earlier. This is the gatekeeper question; no downstream questions exist.

exhaustive_declaration.justification: Ohio County Death Record (original, primary information, direct evidence) gives date 11 Mar 1903 and place Cincinnati, Hamilton, Ohio with high confidence. 1910 census absence independently brackets death before April 1910. No conflicts. Parents Gerhard Ferber and Eva Ferber match tree exactly, confirming correct identification. Remaining plan fallbacks (pli_004–pli_009) are supplementary; no unsearched source is likely to contradict the established date or place.

items.rationale: Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001 (collection 2128172). Hamilton County maintained local death registration from 1865, predating Ohio statewide registration (1908). This indexed collection is the highest-probability source for William's death if he died in Cincinnati before or after statehood registration began. Should return date, place, and informant.

1910 U.S. Census (FamilySearch). William appears alive in 1900. If he is present in the 1910 household — or absent from Emma's household — it brackets his death date before or after April 1910. Emma and son Charles both have 1910 residence entries for Cincinnati Ward 21; if William is absent, he died before 1910. If present, death was post-1910.

Ohio, Deaths, 1908-1953 (collection 1307272). Statewide death certificate series with images. If William survived to 1908 or later, the certificate would give precise date, place, cause, informant, and parents. Fallback to this after county records if q_001 is not yet answered.

Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 (collection 1681000) and Ohio, Church and Civil Deaths, 1833-1991 (collection 2373723). Compiled indexes drawn from multiple sources including church burial records; may capture deaths missed by the county civil registration system, particularly for German Lutheran or Catholic congregations common among Cincinnati's German-American community.

Spring Grove Cemetery burial records and FindAGrave. William's mother Eva Engermann Ferber (d. 1872) is buried at Spring Grove; Emma Ferber (d. 1948) and son Charles (d. 1967) are also interred there. The family has a clear Spring Grove affiliation. A burial record would give exact death date and place and may note cause. FindAGrave (findagrave.com) and Spring Grove's online search (springgrove.org) are accessible without subscription.

Cincinnati newspaper obituaries via Newspapers.com or GenealogyBank. The Ferber family is middle-class Cincinnati German-American; an obituary is plausible in the Cincinnati Enquirer, Cincinnati Post, or the German-language Volksblatt/Freie Presse. An obituary would give exact death date, cause, survivors, and often a burial notice. Search Newspapers.com (external site, requires search-external-sites skill).

Ohio, Hamilton County Records, 1791-1994 (collection 2141016) — browse-only image collection (1.5M images, essentially no indexed records). Contains miscellaneous Hamilton County records that may include death registers or coroner's records not indexed elsewhere. Use search-images skill to browse relevant volumes if indexed searches fail.

Ohio, Hamilton, Cincinnati, Vine Street Hill Cemetery Index (collection 3714673) — indexed Cincinnati cemetery with 60,000+ records. Secondary to Spring Grove check but covers a major Cincinnati burial ground used by German families. Would confirm date and place of death.

Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 (collection 1992421) — Hamilton County probate estate files. A will or administration for William Ferber would give exact death date and would name heirs (confirming relationship to Emma and Charles). Browse-only but volume_search can identify the relevant film. FAN item: also check for Gerhard Ferber (father, d. 1917) whose probate may mention William.

proof_summaries.narrative_markdown:
## Death of William H. Ferber: Proof Summary

**Research Question:** When and where did William H. Ferber (born December 1869, Ohio; husband of Emma Becker Ferber; father of Charles Hubert Ferber, b. 22 June 1891, Cincinnati, Ohio) die?

**Conclusion:** The evidence indicates that William H. Ferber died on **11 March 1903** in **Cincinnati, Hamilton County, Ohio**.

### Primary Evidence

**Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001 (original source).** A death-register entry for "Wm. Ferber" — male, married, white, born about 1870 in Cincinnati, Hamilton, Ohio — records his death on 11 March 1903 in Cincinnati, Hamilton County, Ohio. "Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:F66M-8JZ : accessed 28 July 2026), entry for Wm. Ferber and Gerhard Ferber, 11 Mar 1903; image, https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HT-66TS-SCS.

This is an **original source** — Hamilton County maintained local death registration from 1865, predating Ohio's 1908 statewide requirement. The death date and place constitute **direct evidence** recorded as **primary information**: the entry was created by officials on official duty at or near the time of death (source classified: original / primary / direct).

The record names the decedent's father as **Gerhard Ferber** and his mother as **Eva Ferber**, matching exactly the tree persons GCD9-9X1 (Gerhard Ferber, born 29 September 1820 in Germany, died 31 May 1917 in Cincinnati) and G7J1-QF2 (Eva Engermann Ferber, born 1834 in Bavaria, died 1 January 1872 in Cincinnati). The parental match, together with the matching birth year (~1870 vs. the tree's December 1869) and residence place (Cincinnati, Hamilton County), confirms that this record concerns the correct William H. Ferber and not a namesake. The next-highest-ranked candidate returned by the search scored 0.286 — a different individual — eliminating identity ambiguity.

### Corroborating Evidence

**1910 U.S. Census, Hamilton County, Ohio (negative evidence).** A search of the 1910 federal census for William Ferber in Hamilton County returned no result. William's wife Emma Ferber and son Charles Hubert Ferber are documented in Cincinnati Ward 21, Hamilton County, in 1910. William's absence from that household is **independent negative evidence** — produced by a different record type and creation process — corroborating the 1903 death date. This negative evidence does not independently establish the specific date of death; it establishes that William was not living in April 1910, consistent with the death record.

### Apparent Discrepancy: City Directory Entries, 1904–1910

Cincinnati city directories from 1904 through 1910 are indexed on FamilySearch as pairing "Wm Ferber" or "Wm" with Emma Ferber as a couple. Three of these entries were read directly: the 1904 directory (src_002, ark:/61903/1:1:682V-ZH49), the 1905 directory (src_003, ark:/61903/1:1:6Z5Z-5FPG), and the 1910 directory (src_004, ark:/61903/1:1:6ZYK-RSPD).

In each case the FamilySearch GedcomX confirms that **Emma Ferber is the primary person holding the annual residence fact**, while "Wm Ferber" or "Wm" is indexed as a secondary person **with no independent facts** — no residence claim, no date of any kind. In the 1905 and 1910 entries the surname is entirely absent from the "Wm" entry, a further marker of the widow-entry format (e.g., "Ferber Emma wid Wm") in which the surname is implicit and the husband is named only to identify the widow, not listed as a living resident.

These entries were classified as derivative sources with indeterminate information quality and negative evidence type for the research question (a_008, a_009, a_010). They do not record William as a living Cincinnati resident in any of those years. The pattern is consistent with and corroborates the 11 March 1903 death date; no conflict exists.

### Confidence Assessment

The conclusion reaches **probable** rather than proved because research produced one original source directly and positively stating the death date and place, supplemented by independent negative corroboration from the 1910 census and the three examined city directory entries. The Genealogical Proof Standard's "proved" threshold requires two or more independent original sources with primary information agreeing on the conclusion. A Spring Grove Cemetery burial record, a Cincinnati newspaper obituary, or a Hamilton County probate record would provide a second independent positive source and advance this conclusion to proved. No conflicts were identified. Research was declared reasonably exhaustive.

**Tier: Probable**
